title: Leading around a known void

feedback.title: Leading your ace into a known void
feedback.summary: You lead this trick, and West acts last in it. The earlier trick shows West already void in Clubs, so leading the ace of Clubs offers West a free chance to trump it with any Heart.
points: The earlier trick shows West playing a Diamond when Clubs were led, so West holds no more Clubs this hand.
West acts last in this new trick too, so nothing you lead is safe from a seat you already know is void in it, if West chooses to trump.

You need one more of the two remaining tricks, not both — losing this specific trick does not eliminate the target, it shifts the requirement onto the final trick and the ace still in hand. A different lead reaches for that same one needed trick without this specific, already-confirmed exposure.

feedback.title: Avoid the one confirmed risk on the table
feedback.summary: Leading Diamonds instead avoids West's known Club void entirely. Nothing shown here confirms Diamonds carry any comparable exposure.
points: West's void is specifically in Clubs; leading a different suit does not hand West a free, already-confirmed opportunity to trump.

West's discard in the earlier trick was itself a Diamond, so West held at least one at that point — this does not guarantee West still holds one now, but it is not the confirmed exposure that Clubs are.
You need one more of the two remaining tricks, not both. The ace of Clubs is not spent here; it stays available for the final trick, where West's confirmed Club void will not apply.

author_notes: EC-055 checkpoint-3 coverage: a fifth void-tracking scenario, and the first where South leads (current_trick is empty) rather than responds. play_void_tracking_001/002/004 are all about playing into an already-started trick; the tactical question here is different in kind: which suit to lead, given a known void for the seat that will act last in the new trick. Rotation from South leading is South-East-North-West, so West (the known void seat) is last to act, mirroring the structural risk in play_void_tracking_001 but at the leading decision rather than the following one. No claim is made that Diamonds are safe beyond the absence of contrary evidence. Corrected during owner review (checkpoint 3 closure): the observed trick originally had West trump the led Club with 5H and South follow low with 2C, which per the confirmed trick-winner rule (game_rules_v1) means West actually won that trick, contradicting the authored leader of South for this one. Changed West's discard to a non-trump 3D and South's card to the winning KC (South's own Ace of Clubs, still held now, was never played there) so South legitimately wins the shown trick and leading it next is game-consistent, while West's Club void — the evidence this scenario trains — is unchanged. See lib/core/game_rules/trick_winner.dart, the pure helper added to check this class of error, and this file's own targeted regression test in test/scenarios/play_scenario_test.dart proving the shown trick's winner matches the authored leader here — this is not enforced generically by PlaySituation, since observed_tricks is not guaranteed to be the immediately previous trick (see docs/DECISIONS.md D-025). Corrected again during the owner's target-feasibility review: with the original tricks_taken (south 2 of 4, two cards remaining), South needed both remaining tricks (mustWinAll per lib/core/game_rules/target_feasibility.dart), yet the authored 4D — a low card with no case for winning on its own — was rated Strong over the Ace, which would win outright except for the one confirmed, named risk. Preferring the card with no winning case at all in a must-win-every-remaining-trick state was not a defensible reading of the exact-target objective, void evidence or not. Rebalanced tricks_taken to south 3 of 4 (need one more of two remaining, not both) and north 2 of 4 to keep the total at 11 completed tricks (13 minus the 2-card remaining hand); no scenario content referenced any specific opponent's taken count, so this rebalance changes nothing else about the lesson. Under this corrected state (slack, not mustWinAll), preferring the safer lead over the higher-card-but-exposed one is a genuine, defensible trade-off — the same shape play_void_tracking_001 already uses — since losing this trick still leaves the ace available for the one remaining trick after it. Both evaluations' points now say this explicitly rather than leaving it implicit.
